topics.title: US Saudi Nuclear Deal
bullets: On 22 July 2026, the US and Saudi Arabia signed a civilian nuclear cooperation agreement, known as a "123 Agreement", along with a bilateral safeguards agreement.
The deal establishes a 30-year, multi-billion-dollar partnership allowing US companies to develop Saudi Arabia's civilian nuclear infrastructure.
President Trump later conditioned the deal on Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing relations with Israel, casting its future into doubt Background –
A "123 Agreement" refers to Section 123 of the US Atomic Energy Act, governing the transfer of US civilian nuclear technology to foreign countries.
It establishes the legal framework for US companies to build and operate nuclear facilities in partner countries, with safeguards and monitoring.
The deal goes to Congress for 90 session days; opponents need a two-thirds majority to override a presidential veto.
In 2009, the US signed a similar nuclear agreement with the United Arab Emirates (UAE) , which became known as the "gold standard" for nuclear cooperation.
The UAE permanently renounced domestic uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing, agreed to import nuclear fuel, and adopted the IAEA's Additional Protocol for intrusive inspections .
The Saudi deal reportedly does not include these restrictions, allowing Riyadh to retain the option to enrich uranium domestically .
Saudi Arabia is a signatory to the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT), which commits non-nuclear states to forgo developing nuclear weapons.
As an NPT member, Saudi Arabia's nuclear program remains subject to IAEA inspections .
However, the deal does not require Riyadh to sign the Additional Protocol, which allows for stricter, "snap" inspections of nuclear facilities.
Saudi Arabia's nuclear power program is part of Vision 2030, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman's economic diversification plan aimed at reducing the kingdom's dependence on oil.
By using nuclear energy for electricity generation, Saudi Arabia can free up more oil for export, boosting revenues while reducing domestic carbon emissions .
Riyadh has long warned that if it could not partner with the US, it would turn to China or Russia, which have different proliferation standards.
In a 2018 interview, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman stated that Saudi Arabia "without a doubt" would develop a nuclear weapon if Iran acquired one.
The deal comes amid a US-Israel war with Iran, which is being fought in part to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons capability .
In September 2025, Saudi Arabia signed a mutual defence pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan .
Pakistan's Defence Minister later stated that Islamabad's nuclear programme "will be made available" to Riyadh if required.
This pact has further heightened concerns about nuclear proliferation in the Middle East and Saudi Arabia's potential access to weapons technology. Recent News –
The 30-year agreement is designed to "meet the energy needs" of Saudi Arabia while giving US companies "great access" to the kingdom's nuclear program .
The deal paves the way for US firms to build and operate nuclear reactors in Saudi Arabia, potentially worth tens of billions of dollars .
It also reportedly includes provisions for a joint two-year feasibility study examining the commercial viability of domestic uranium enrichment in Saudi Arabia .
Under the agreement, Saudi Arabia could potentially build a uranium enrichment facility on its soil, pending the outcome of the two-year joint study .
Any enrichment would be done under a "black box" arrangement meant to prevent the transfer of sensitive enrichment technology to Saudi Arabia, according to officials .
Critics argue that the same centrifuges used to produce low-enriched fuel for reactors can also produce weapons-grade uranium if operated for longer periods .
Unlike previous US nuclear agreements, the Saudi deal does not require Riyadh to sign the IAEA's Additional Protocol .
The Additional Protocol gives inspectors broader powers to conduct "snap inspections" and investigate suspected undeclared sites .
Saudi Arabia has reportedly refused to accept this requirement.
On 24 July 2026, President Trump stated that the nuclear deal would be "totally subject" to Saudi Arabia joining the Abraham Accords and normalizing relations with Israel .
He also added that there would be "no enrichment of material" under the agreement .
Riyadh has so far resisted joining the Abraham Accords, which were brokered by Trump in his first term and signed by the UAE, Bahrain, Morocco, and Sudan . Abraham Accords –
The Abraham Accords are a series of US-brokered diplomatic agreements signed in 2020 that established formal relations between Israel and several Arab nations .
The first agreements were signed at the White House on September 15, 2020, between Israel and the United Arab Emirates (UAE) and Bahrain .
Before 2020, only Egypt (1979) and Jordan (1994) had formally recognised Israel among Arab nations .
Most Arab states had long maintained they would not establish ties with Israel until a Palestinian state was created .
Before the Accords, Israeli citizens could not travel to Gulf states, and even direct phone calls to Israel were blocked in some Arab countries .
Morocco and Sudan joined the Accords in 2020 and 2021 .
Kazakhstan became the first post-Soviet state to join in November 2025 .
Saudi Arabia has so far resisted joining, insisting on a clear pathway to Palestinian statehood . Non-Proliferation Treaty –
The Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons (NPT) is a landmark international treaty opened for signature in 1968 and entered into force in March 1970 .
Its objective is to prevent the spread of nuclear weapons and weapons technology, promote cooperation in the peaceful uses of nuclear energy, and further the goal of nuclear disarmament .
With 191 states parties, it has the widest adherence to any arms control agreement .
The NPT is built on a "grand bargain" resting on three pillars: non-proliferation, peaceful use of nuclear energy, and nuclear disarmament .
Non-nuclear-weapon states (NNWS) agree to forgo developing or acquiring nuclear weapons (Article II), while nuclear-weapon states (NWS) agree not to transfer nuclear weapons technology (Article I) .

The treaty also enshrines the "inalienable right" of all states to develop nuclear energy for peaceful purposes (Article IV) and commits states to pursue nuclear disarmament in good faith (Article VI) .
The NPT recognizes only five Nuclear-Weapon States (NWS) : the United States, Russia, China, France, and the United Kingdom – countries that exploded a nuclear device before 1 January 1967 .
All other state parties are classified as Non-Nuclear-Weapon States (NNWS) and have pledged to forswear nuclear weapons .
India, Israel, Pakistan, and South Sudan have never signed the treaty; North Korea announced withdrawal in 2003 .
Article III requires NNWS to accept IAEA safeguards to verify that nuclear materials are not diverted for weapons purposes .
Article X gives states the right to withdraw if "extraordinary events" jeopardize their supreme interests, with three months' notice .
North Korea is the only state to have withdrawn; its legal status remains contested .
In 1995, states parties agreed to extend the treaty indefinitely .
The treaty requires a Review Conference every five years to assess implementation and strengthen the treaty .
The 2026 Review Conference (April–May) failed to adopt a consensus final document – the third consecutive failure (following 2015 and 2022) . IAEA –
The International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) is an autonomous intergovernmental organization established to promote the peaceful use of nuclear energy and prevent its use for military purposes.
It was created following U.S. President Eisenhower’s "Atoms for Peace" address to the UN General Assembly on 8 December 1953, and its statute came into force on 29 July 1957.
The IAEA is headquartered in Vienna, Austria, and has regional offices in Toronto, Tokyo, and liaison offices in New York and Geneva.
The IAEA's primary mission is nuclear verification – it applies safeguards to ensure that nuclear material is not diverted from peaceful uses to weapons programs.
Under the NPT, all non-nuclear-weapon states are required to conclude a Comprehensive Safeguards Agreement (CSA) with the IAEA, allowing inspections of declared nuclear facilities.

The Additional Protocol (1997) strengthens the IAEA's ability to detect undeclared nuclear activities by granting expanded access to information and locations; as of 2025, it is in force with 144 states.

topics.title: Ken-Betwa Project
bullets: On 19 July 2026, MP Police cleared a 15-day Ken-Betwa protest at Kupi village, detaining leader Amit Bhatnagar (on hunger strike for 14 days) and 150 protesters.
Bhatnagar was hospitalised due to deteriorating health; protesters staged 'jal satyagraha', 'chita satyagraha' and symbolic 'faansi satyagraha' .
The protest highlighted grievances over land acquisition, rehabilitation, compensation irregularities, and environmental concerns Background –
The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is India's first river interlinking project under the National Perspective Plan (NPP).
It aims to transfer surplus water from the Ken river to the Betwa basin through the Daudhan Dam and a 221-km canal.
The project will provide irrigation, drinking water, and hydropower across Madhya Pradesh and Uttar Pradesh.
The Union Cabinet cleared the project in December 2021 at an estimated cost of ₹44,605 crore .
The foundation stone was laid in December 2024.
The project will submerge 6,017 hectares of forest, affect 7,193 families, and provide irrigation to 10 lakh hectares and drinking water to 62 lakh people. About the Project –
The project aims to provide irrigation to more than 10 lakh hectares of farmland in the drought-prone Bundelkhand region.
It will provide drinking water to approximately 62 lakh people and generate hydroelectric power.
The government has described the project as a major development initiative to address water shortages and boost economic growth in the region.
The project involves the construction of a 77-metre-high Daudhan Dam on the Ken river in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh .
The link canal will have a length of 221 km, including a 2 km tunnel .
Two power projects have also been proposed as part of the project .
Under the displacement policy, affected families are entitled to ₹12.5 lakh per adult as compensation.
If a person opts for a plot, ₹5 lakh will be deducted from the compensation, and the remaining ₹7.5 lakh will be given in cash.
The state government has sanctioned an additional ₹202.5 crore for rehabilitation, increasing assistance from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per eligible family.
The project will affect approximately 6,017 hectares of forest area in and around the Panna Tiger Reserve (PTR).
Around 17,101 trees have been identified for felling, of which 12,404 trees have already been felled within the Panna Tiger Reserve.
The project will also impact the Ken Gharial Sanctuary and submerge nearly 98 sq km of the tiger reserve.
An Integrated Landscape Management Plan (ILMP) has been prepared by the Wildlife Institute of India (WII) to mitigate the environmental impact .
The ILMP aims to improve habitat quality, maintain critical wildlife corridors linking adjacent Protected Areas, and protect flagship species – including tigers, vultures, and gharials .
A Greater Panna Landscape Council (GPLC) has been constituted under the chairmanship of the Chief Secretary of Madhya Pradesh to ensure systematic implementation of the ILMP .
A Central Empowered Committee (CEC) was constituted by the Supreme Court to examine the wildlife clearance for the project.
The CEC raised concerns about the project's impact on the ecological integrity of Panna Tiger Reserve and recommended studies on mitigative measures.

The Forest Advisory Committee (FAC) and environmental experts have warned that the project will involve felling of approx. 46 lakh trees (each with a girth greater than 20 cm) from the forest area alone. National Perspective Plan –
The NPP was formulated in 1980 by the Ministry of Irrigation (now Jal Shakti) for inter-basin transfer of water from surplus to deficit basins.
It aims to mitigate floods and droughts by diverting flood water to water-short regions and recharging groundwater.
The National Water Development Agency (NWDA), set up in 1982, is responsible for implementing the ILR programme under the NPP.
The NPP comprises 30 identified interlinking projects: 16 under the Peninsular Component and 14 under the Himalayan Component.
Peninsular Component includes links like Ken-Betwa, Godavari-Krishna, and Krishna-Pennar.
Himalayan Component includes projects like Kosi-Ghaghra, Gandak-Ganga, and Ghaghra-Yamuna.
Pre-Feasibility Reports (PFRs) have been completed for all 30 projects.
Feasibility Reports (FRs) have been finalised for 26 projects.
Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) have been prepared for 13 projects (as of Dec 2025).
The government has identified five priority projects: Ken-Betwa Link, Modified Parbati-Kalisindh-Chambal (PKC) Link, and three sub-links under the Godavari-Cauvery Link.
The Ken-Betwa Link Project (KBLP) is the first and only project under implementation.
The Godavari-Cauvery Link consists of: Godavari (Inchampalli)– Krishna (Nagarjunasagar), Krishna (Nagarjunasagar)–Pennar (Somasila), and Pennar (Somasila)–Cauvery (Grand Anicut). Recent News –
On 19 July 2026, MP Police cleared a 15-day protest against the Ken-Betwa Link Project at Kupi village in Chhatarpur district.
The protest began on 3 July 2026 on the banks of the Barana river near Kupi village in Chhatarpur district, Madhya Pradesh.
Protest leader Amit Bhatnagar, who was on an indefinite hunger strike for 14 days, was hospitalised due to deteriorating health.

The protest, led largely by tribal women, featured symbolic demonstrations including 'jal satyagraha' (water protest), 'chita satyagraha' (funeral pyre protest), and symbolic 'faansi satyagraha' (hanging protest).
Protesters raised the slogan "nyaya do ya maar do" (give justice or kill us), dramatising the "death" of villages facing submergence.
Visuals of women lying on symbolic pyres and placing nooses around their necks drew national attention on social media.
Amit Bhatnagar, founder of Jai Kisan Sangathan, led the agitation and had been on an indefinite hunger strike for 14 days.
Bhatnagar is a social activist who has worked on displacement and rehabilitation issues in Bundelkhand for several years.
Protest leader Divya Ahirwar alleged that Bhatnagar was detained before he could address the media on "corruption of Rs 400 crore" in the project.
Bhatnagar alleged "irregularities" in compensation disbursement, claiming that gram sabha proceedings were fabricated and that ₹8 crore of ₹11 crore was paid to ineligible individuals.
He alleged ₹400 crore corruption in the project, including the inclusion of fake beneficiaries in compensation lists.
Protesters demanded that the rehabilitation package be increased from ₹5 lakh to ₹12.5 lakh per family, and that the cut-off date for eligibility be extended.
Chhatarpur Collector Parth Jaiswal rejected the allegations, stating that 90% of protesters were not project-affected and had come from Panna district with grievances about other projects.
Police justified the action citing safety risks as the protest was staged beneath a bridge and in the river, with water levels rising.
The administration stated that the project is of national importance and will boost irrigation, drinking water supply, and development in Bundelkhand. Other Major River Disputes –
The Cauvery water dispute is one of India's oldest and most contentious inter-State river water conflicts, involving Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, and Puducherry .
The conflict originated during the British colonial period, with agreements signed in 1892 and 1924 between the Madras Presidency and the princely state of Mysore .
The Supreme Court delivered its landmark judgment on 16 February 2018, modifying the Cauvery Water Disputes Tribunal award.
Several inter-State disputes exist over the sharing of waters of the Godavari and Krishna rivers, involving states like Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Karnataka, and Maharashtra.
The Polavaram Project on the Godavari has been a source of contention between Andhra Pradesh and neighbouring states.
The Government of India has approved the Revised Cost Estimate of ₹30,436 crore for the Polavaram Project with additional central assistance.
The Narmada Water Dispute involves Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Rajasthan.
The dispute was adjudicated by the Narmada Water Disputes Tribunal, which delivered its award in 1979.
The Narmada Bachao Andolan (Save Narmada Movement) was a major social movement opposing the construction of large dams on the Narmada river.
The Ravi-Beas water dispute involves Punjab, Haryana, and Rajasthan.
The dispute arose after the reorganisation of Punjab in 1966, when the waters of the Ravi and Beas rivers had to be shared.
The dispute remains unresolved, with multiple rounds of negotiations and legal proceedings.
